1001947.etyen: From Latvian Jūrmala (“Jūrmala”), from jūrmala (“seaside”), itself a compound from jūra (“sea”) + mala (“edge, shore”), first part from Proto-Baltic or Proto-Balto-Slavic *jaur-, *jūr-, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂wer-, *ūr- with an added initial y, from *aw-, *awe- (“to wet, to moisten, to flow”) with a suffix -r + last part from Proto-Indo-European *ml̥Hdʰo-.

en.g: a surname originating as a patronymic, originally meaning “son of Magnus”

1002715.etyen:
From Magnus (“male given name”) + -sen (“patronymic suffix meaning “son of””), originally a patronymic meaning “son of Magnus”. The given name Magnus ultimately derives from Latin magnus (“great, large”).
Compare Danish Magnussen, German Magnussen, Norwegian Nynorsk Magnusson, Swedish Magnusson, Icelandic Magnússon and Faroese Magnusson (“patronymic surname”).

1004763.etyen:
From suppe (“soup”) + bolle (“bowl”), literally “soup bowl”.
Parallel formations include Swedish soppskål, German Suppenschüssel, Dutch soepkom, English soup bowl, Korean 국그릇 (gukgeureut) and Japanese 汁椀 (“soup bowl”).

disse kongsfrænders fordring paa Borgesyssel som personligt len
these royal kinsmen's claim to Borgesyssel as a personal fief

1005019.etyen:
Compound of konge (“king”) + frende (“kinsman, relative”), with the fossilized genitival linking form kongs-, literally “king's kinsman”. The compound continues konungsfrændi (“king's kinsman, royal relative”), formed from the genitive singular konungs (“king”) + frændi (“kinsman, relative”).
The first element konge is from Old Norse konungr (“king”), from Proto-Germanic *kuningaz (“king”), derived from *kunją (“kin, family, clan”) with *-ingaz (“suffix indicating belonging”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ǵenh₁- (“to produce, beget, give birth”).
